A determined boundary may be surveyed using measurements from permanent features.
A determined boundary may alternatively be surveyed using Ordnance Survey National Grid coordinates.
National Grid coordinates are most appropriate where suitable permanent features are scarce or taped distances would be excessive.
Coordinate-based determination requires specialist surveying equipment.
The exact boundary does not have to be marked on the ground by a fence or wall.
Permanent ground markers can be used where a physical boundary feature is absent.
The plan must clearly show the extent to be determined by suitable colouring, edging or another reference.
The plan must identify the start, end and any turning points, preferably with lettered points.
The plan must contain a statement describing the exact line to be determined.
The plan must show surrounding detail and orientation such as a north point.
The preferred determined-boundary plan scale is no smaller than 1:200.
The determined-boundary plan should ideally be no larger than A3.
The plan must not carry a disclaimer that casts doubt on its accuracy.
Measurements on the plan must be accurate to plus or minus 10 millimetres.
Measurements must be horizontal rather than measured along a slope.
Measurements must be taken from at least two defined points on permanent surrounding features.
A permanent feature is one reasonably expected to remain in position for at least ten years.
Flood zones are an Environment Agency guide to the probability of river and sea flooding in England.
Flood zone 1 is the least likely to flood and flood zone 3 is more likely to flood.
A flood zone does not establish that a location will definitely flood.
A flood zone does not state the severity of any future flood.
